PURPOSE. Heading III: Atg 1/5 = (1) - (13). This continues the previous page (II: Atg 1/70 = 2(1) - 2(13) - (29)). (p) denotes the argument of the Gaussian prime of norm p: (1) = arg(1+i) = pi/4, (13) = arg(3+2i) = arctan(2/3), (29) = arg(5+2i) = arctan(2/5). Since 5+i = (1+i)(3-2i), we get arctan(1/5) = pi/4 - arctan(2/3), which the heading writes as (1) - (13). The page evaluates arctan(1/5) by its Gregory series to 60 decimals. Together with values like arctan(1/70) on the previous page, this yields the 'prime angles' (13), (29), ... to high precision. It is the angular analogue of tabulating logarithms of primes.

METHOD. arctan(1/5) = P - N.
- Positive terms: P = sum over k = 1, 5, 9, ... of 1/(k*5^k).
- Negative terms: N = sum over k = 3, 7, 11, ... of 1/(k*5^k).
- Each term is written as 1/(k*5^k) = 2^k/(k*10^k), so it is just the repeating decimal of 2^k/k shifted k places.
- Gauss groups terms whose 1/k have decimal periods dividing a common length L. The marginal labels '(L' are these periods, so each group sum can be written as an exact repeating decimal.
- All numbers are 60-decimal fixed-point values written in blocks of 10 digits. Partial sums often show only the trailing blocks.

results.what: arctan(1/5) = pi/4 - arctan(2/3), via the factorization 5+i = (1+i)(3-2i), written in Gauss's notation for arguments of Gaussian primes ((1), (13), (29)).
results.modern_name: Gaussian-integer decomposition of arctangents (basis of Machin-like formula theory)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass, Werke II); later systematized by Störmer (1896) and Todd (1949)

results.what: 60-decimal evaluation of arctan(1/5) by the Gregory series, with terms as 2^k/(k*10^k) and positive/negative terms summed separately.
results.modern_name: Gregory–Leibniz arctangent series, high-precision fixed-point evaluation
results.usually_credited_to: Gregory/Leibniz (series); Machin, Euler, Vega et al. (high-precision use)

results.what: Grouping series terms by the decimal period of 1/k, so that group sums are exact repeating decimals (period labels 18, 22, 15, 6, 16, 28, 30, 1, 42).
results.modern_name: computational bookkeeping using periods of decimal fractions (multiplicative order of 10 mod k)
results.usually_credited_to: unsure; Gauss's interest in decimal periods is documented in Disquisitiones (1801) and his period tables

deep.surprise_reason: High-precision arctangent evaluations for Gaussian-prime angles belong to Gauss's known Nachlass work on arctangent relations (Werke II). The computation is correct to 60 places and the period-grouping trick is a nice detail, but nothing here is new mathematics.
